transcript.text:
Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining this litigation-planning meeting. As you all know, we're defending a trade-secrets misappropriation suit brought by a former employee, and the complaint is seeking broad inspection of our devices and systems. We have an initial case-management conference coming up next month, and no discovery has been exchanged yet. Our priorities are clear: protect the company's confidential information and keep defense costs under control.

Before I approve the initial defense plan, I need both of you to identify any facts that should shape our approach. Discovery counsel, what do we need to know on the e-discovery and information-protection front? And insurance-coverage counsel, what should we be aware of on the coverage side? Please walk me through anything that could affect our strategy.

transcript.text: Elena, I have a critical fact that should significantly shape our initial defense plan. My forensic review of the former employee's company laptop has been completed, and the findings are quite targeted: exactly three identified trade-secret files were copied to the device. Importantly, the review found no customer data on the laptop and no evidence of any additional copying beyond those three files. This is significant because it allows us to push back against the broad inspection demands in the complaint with concrete, specific evidence — we can argue that discovery should be scoped to those three files rather than opening up our entire systems. My report is currently awaiting final partner review and hasn't yet been added to the case plan, but I wanted you to have this information now so it can inform our strategy heading into the case-management conference.

transcript.text: Elena, on the coverage side, I've reviewed the applicable policy endorsement and there are three key points that should shape our defense plan. First, the trade-secret defense is covered, but subject to a $75,000 self-insured retention. Second, we must use insurer-approved panel counsel. Third, we need written insurer consent before engaging any forensic vendor. That last point is critical given Samir's forensic review — we need to make sure that work is aligned with the endorsement requirements, or we risk coverage issues. I should also note that this endorsement is currently stored in the risk department's file and has not yet been attached to this matter, so we need to get it into the case file promptly.
